title: Al-'Aziz, the Almighty
hookLine: the Almighty, whom none can overcome, and a short sentence for the weak moment
tomorrow: the Almighty can't be overcome. so why is His next name about mending?

cards: The deadline is tomorrow. The form is open, the cursor blinking, and suddenly nothing works: can't decide, can't even pick what to eat. A weak moment doesn't ask permission.

Today's name is for exactly that moment: Al-'Aziz, the Almighty, the one none can overcome. In Pickthall's list from Surah al-Hashr it's the Majestic, and the surah closes with it: He is the Mighty, the Wise.

teach.b: So what does a person in a weak moment do with a God nothing can defeat? The tradition hands over a short sentence: Hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil. Allah is enough for us, and He is the best one to trust.
It's in the Qur'an, in Surah Al Imran, said by people who'd just been told an army had gathered against them, so be afraid.
And Bukhari records Ibn Abbas saying who said it first: Ibrahim, when he was thrown into the fire, and Muhammad, peace be upon him, when he heard about that army.
Two of the hardest moments in the story, the same short sentence. Notice what kind of sentence it is.
It isn't a claim of strength. It's the opposite: I'm not enough here, and He is.
The weakness gets said out loud, and then leaned on something that can't be overcome.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the sentence Ibrahim said in the fire is short enough to say in a storeroom with your face in your hands. Al-'Aziz doesn't need you to be strong.
That's what the might is for.

how: Muslims say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil, Allah is enough for us and the best to trust, in moments of fear or pressure, often under the breath.

o: the Almighty, whom no one can overcome
the Wise, who knows what is best for you
the Beloved, who loves the ones who pray

games.q: the weak moment — tap the pairs.
p: said it thrown into the fire
said it when an army gathered

s: saying hasbunallah is a way of claiming to be strong
it's the opposite: I'm not enough here, and He is.
Bukhari records that Ibrahim said it when he was thrown into the fire
Ibn Abbas reports it, and that Muhammad said it when told an army had gathered.
strong faith means never having a weak moment
the sentence was said in the hardest moments of the story, by people who'd just been told to be afraid.

games.q: your best friend failed her driving test twice and says she's 'just weak.' she's scared to book again. what does hasbunallah offer her?
o: admit it's hard, lean on the One none can overcome, and book the next one.
real faith would mean she wouldn't feel any fear about it at all.
failing twice is a sign it isn't meant for her, so she can stop.
games.why: Allah is enough for us: said by people who were weak and afraid, and then they went forward anyway.

practice: Close your eyes and let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, the posture of someone who isn't holding everything up alone.
If you pray, you might say hasbunallah silently on each out-breath; if not, let each breath out be a small setting-down. Stay there for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-'Aziz: the Almighty, the one none can overcome, the might a weak moment can lean on.

orig.note: Arabic: the Almighty, the Mighty, the one who cannot be overcome.

carryVoice: Keep this one: his might, for the moments when mine runs all the way out. Day by day.

sources.ref: Qur'an 59:23-24 (al-'Aziz: 'the Majestic' in the list; the surah closes 'He is the Mighty, the Wise')
sources.q: He is the Mighty, the Wise

sources.ref: Qur'an 3:173 (told an army has gathered, so fear them, they said: Allah is sufficient for us, the best to trust)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4563 (Ibn Abbas: hasbuna Allah wa ni'ma al-wakil was said by Ibrahim when thrown into the fire, and by Muhammad when told the people had gathered against them)
